header.title: GDPR and other data laws, clearly and step by step
header.lead: What the law requires, when to start, which law applies in which country and what it costs. For developers and small products. Checked against sources on 17 November 2026.

legend.inference: follows from the sources, not stated outright

hero.title: You can’t “get” compliance. It is a state you must be able to prove at any moment
hero.lead: There is no license, registration or mandatory certificate. You pay for four things to exist and to match reality.
pillars: Documentsrecords, privacy policy, DPAs; a DPIA when risk is high

applies.title: When GDPR starts to apply to you
applies.text: If you have an establishment in the EU, deliberately offer goods or services to people in the EU, or monitor their behavior there (Art. 3). Then one customer is enough. A chance visitor from the EU does not bring you in, as long as you neither target the EU nor track people there. There is no exemption for small companies. [data https://gdpr-info.eu/art-3-gdpr/]

urgent.title: When it becomes urgent [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-28-gdpr/]
items: your first B2B customer in the EU sends a DPA and a security questionnaire;
pixels and analytics on EU traffic;
special-category data or children’s data;
your first breach.

verdicts.title: Your own badge
verdicts.text: There is not and never was an official EU logo. A home-made badge has no legal weight. [data https://www.complyjet.com/blog/gdpr-logo]

verdicts.title: “Certified” without a certificate
verdicts.text: Misleading: in Luxembourg, a “CNPD certified” label without a valid GDPR-CARPA certificate is treated as exactly that. [data https://luxgap.com/lois/rgpd/cons-100/?lang=en]

verdicts.title: Certificate under Art. 42
verdicts.text: Europrivacy and others: voluntary, only through an accredited body, covers the listed operations rather than the whole company. EDPB: a certificate does not mean full compliance. [data https://www.clym.io/blog/edpb-approves-first-european-data-protection-seals-what-it-means-for-your-gdpr-compliance]

verdicts.title: What actually works
verdicts.text: A DPA, a list of subprocessors and a description of security measures: that is what a customer will ask for. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-28-gdpr/]

data.title: Data: the regime depends on the category
data.text: Ordinary data (name, email, IP) needs a legal basis, a clear policy and a retention period. Health, mental state and intimate life usually need explicit consent given as a separate action, and a DPIA; below the age of digital consent, children need a parent’s consent. The most common trap is data from which something sensitive can be inferred: it gets the same strict regime. [data https://connectontech.bakermckenzie.com/sensitive-data-under-the-cjeus-spotlight-practical-implications/]

categories.title: Data categories and what each one needs
categories.lead: The regime depends on what exactly you process, and one app almost always handles several categories at once. The square next to the risk level shows it in color. Fines have two tiers: up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher, and up to €10 million or 2% (Art. 83). [data https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj]

ordinary.title: Ordinary personal data <small>Art. 4(1), 6</small>
ordinary.example: Name, email, IP, device ID, cookie ID, activity history.
ordinary.need: One of 6 legal bases per purpose, a privacy policy, a retention period, DPAs with contractors, user rights.
ordinary.cost: up to 4%legal bases and principles; up to 2%security and documentation.

special.title: Special categories <small>Art. 9</small>
special.example: Health, including mental health; sex life and orientation; biometrics for identification; genetics; ethnic origin; religion; politics; trade union membership.
special.need: A basis from Art. 6 plus an exception from Art. 9(2), for apps usually explicit consent given as a separate action. DPIA, encryption, no third-party trackers nearby.
special.cost: up to 4%a breach is almost always “high risk”: notify the people themselves.

inferred.title: Indirectly sensitive <small>EU Court of Justice case law</small>
inferred.example: Data from which something sensitive can be inferred: a partner’s name (OT case, 2022), a medicine order (Lindenapotheke, 2024).
inferred.need: The same regime as Art. 9. Intent and accuracy of the inference do not matter. [data https://connectontech.bakermckenzie.com/sensitive-data-under-the-cjeus-spotlight-practical-implications/]
inferred.cost: up to 4%the most common trap: assuming that if you never ask about health directly, there are no special categories. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-9-gdpr/]

children.title: Children’s data <small>Art. 8</small>
children.example: Users below the age of digital consent: 16 by default, countries lower it to 13. For example: Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands 16; France 15; Austria, Spain, Italy 14; Belgium, Denmark 13.
children.need: If you rely on consent: a parent’s consent and a reasonable check. Text children can understand, privacy by default.
children.cost: up to 2%under Art. 8; in practice fined together with breaches of principles, and then up to 4% (TikTok, Instagram).

profiling.title: Profiling <small>Art. 4(4), 21, 22</small>
profiling.example: Automated evaluation of personality, behavior, preferences: scoring, types, predictions.
profiling.need: Explain the logic in the privacy policy, give a right to object. A decision with significant effects and no human involved is allowed only under a contract, law or explicit consent. In Switzerland “high-risk profiling” requires express consent.
profiling.cost: up to 4%data-subject rights are in the upper tier.

pseudonymous.title: Pseudonymous and anonymous <small>Art. 4(5), recital 26</small>
pseudonymous.example: Pseudonymous: the key is kept separately, e.g. a hashed email. Anonymous: no reasonable means can single the person out.
pseudonymous.need: Pseudonymous data remains personal data, just with less risk. Anonymous data falls outside GDPR entirely, but small samples are easy to re-identify.
pseudonymous.cost: as for the source dataif “anonymous” data turns out to be re-identifiable.

categories.note: One more category people rarely think of: data on criminal convictions and offences (Art. 10). A private business may process it only where the law expressly allows.
categories.sources: Baker McKenzie on the OT, Meta and Lindenapotheke cases, recital 35, age of consent by country, nFADP Art. 6, GDPR text

example.title: Example breakdown: a psychological test app for two
example.lead: Data logic: a person answers questions about closeness, anxiety, avoidance and attraction; gets a profile on several scales; can invite a second person, and they see a joint result. The operator is in Switzerland, users in Switzerland and the EU, so nFADP and GDPR both apply. The classification below is an inference from the law and EU Court case law. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-9-gdpr/]

anxiety.need: Explicit consent as a separate action before the first question (GDPR Art. 9(2)(a); in Switzerland Art. 6(7)). DPIA. Only the questions you need.
anxiety.wrong: The top fine tier, complaints, compensation claims.

intimacy.need: The same explicit consent. A way to skip a question without breaking the result.
intimacy.wrong: Disclosure to the partner or third parties is a high-risk breach: notify the regulator and the people themselves.

profile.need: Explain in plain words in the privacy policy how the result is calculated. In Switzerland this is probably “high-risk profiling”: an assessment of essential aspects of personality, so again express consent.
profile.wrong: The profile is more sensitive than the answers themselves: in a breach it is the main harm.

joint.need: Consent from each. One person’s answers are not visible to the other without consent. If one deletes their data, their part disappears from the joint result, not just their access.
joint.wrong: The second person is a separate data subject with a right to complain and sue. Compensation for non-material damage needs no seriousness threshold (EU Court, C-300/21). [data https://jonesday.com/en/insights/2023/05/cjeu-clarifies-the-right-to-compensation-for-gdpr-infringements-causing-nonmaterial-damage]

nonUser.data: Answers about a person who didn’t take the test
category: usually not personal data for the operator
nonUser.need: Don’t store the partner’s name, contacts or photo. As long as the operator cannot identify them, it is not their personal data.
nonUser.wrong: A “partner’s name” field turns them into a data subject you must inform under Art. 14.

technical.data: Device ID, invite link, IP during sync
technical.need: Basis: “contract”. Short lifetimes for links and transfer sessions. US hosting: provider’s DPF certification or SCCs.
technical.wrong: A guessed link opens someone else’s result: that is already a breach of special-category data.

age.need: The topic will attract teenagers. Explicit consent to special categories from a minor is doubtful, so set a 16+ or 18+ threshold with age confirmation.
age.wrong: Children plus special categories is the combination regulators fine most readily.

callouts: What lowers risk the most. Keep answers on the device only and don’t send to the server what the joint result doesn’t need. What the operator doesn’t have, it can’t lose.
What’s almost free. A consent screen before the test, a clear privacy policy with the operator’s contact, a “delete for both” button, no analytics on question screens.
A Swiss nuance. For wilful failure to inform, nFADP fines the responsible individual personally, up to CHF 250,000. A company only in exceptional cases.

stages.title: What the law asks at each product stage
stages.lead: The law has no threshold by number of people: duties start with the first person who isn’t you. [data https://gdpr-info.eu/art-2-gdpr/] But what a regulator would actually check, and what is cheaper to do right away, depends a lot on the stage. Find your row; sensitive data and money add requirements at any stage. [inference https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/executive-summary]

prototype.title: Prototype for yourself
prototype.who: only your own or made-up data
cells: Already requiredAlmost nothing by law: personal data for purely personal purposes is outside GDPR (Art. 2(2)(c)). [data https://gdpr-info.eu/art-2-gdpr/]

Do it now while it’s cheapDecide the architecture: what never leaves the device, what is encrypted before sending, which storage region, no third-party analytics. This is the most expensive thing to redo later. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-25-gdpr/]
Next step whenthe first other person appears, even a friend.

closedBeta.title: Closed beta with people you know
closedBeta.who: up to a few dozen people, invite only
cells: Already requiredA short honest text: who you are, what you collect, why, where it is stored, how to delete it. Deletion on request. If questions touch health, intimacy or children, explicit consent with a separate checkbox. No secrets in the repository.

Can waitAn EU representative, the full document set, a lawyer. Formally, records of processing are already required with special categories; a short one takes an hour. A complaint from people you know is unlikely, but the harm from a breach is the same. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-30-gdpr/]
Next step whenstrangers or a public link appear.

openBeta.title: Open beta or free launch
cells: Already requiredA full policy: operator and contact, purposes, bases, recipients and countries, retention, rights, where to complain. DPAs with hosting and services. A consent banner if there are optional cookies or analytics. A breach plan and an incident log. Deletion and export.
If you are outside the EU and users are in the EUA representative under Art. 27 unless the exemption fits (see below). For special categories, a DPIA before launch.
Next step whenyou start charging money or working with companies.

sensitive.title: Sensitive data, at any stage
sensitive.who: health, mental state, intimacy, children, biometrics
cells: From the first userExplicit consent (GDPR Art. 9(2)(a), nFADP Art. 6(7)), only the questions you need, an age threshold of 16+ or 18+, no data to analytics or AI services without separate consent.
Before public launchA DPIA (Art. 35) and records of processing. A breach of such data is almost always “high risk”: notify both the regulator and the people.
What lowers risk the mostdon’t store the answers on a server, or store only ciphertext you hold no key to. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-34-gdpr/]

paid.title: Paid product
cells: AddsTerms of use and a contract, the payment provider as a separate recipient of data, keeping payment records for the tax period. In Switzerland, selling online needs an Impressum: name, postal address and email (UWG art. 3(1)(s)). [data https://www.kmu.admin.ch/de/die-gesetze-der-schweiz-und-der-eu]
Next step whenyour first business customer signs up.

b2b.title: Business customers (B2B)
cells: AddsThe customer will send a DPA and a security questionnaire. You need your own DPA template, a list of subprocessors with regions and a description of security measures. Without them the deal stalls. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-28-gdpr/]

growth.title: Growth or incident
cells: AddsA DPO if your core activity is large-scale processing of special categories or systematic monitoring (Art. 37). Regular review, an external audit. After a breach, 72 hours to notify under GDPR. [data https://gdpr-info.eu/art-37-gdpr/]

stages.example: Example: the couples test app from the breakdown below, in a closed beta, matches the “closed beta” and “sensitive data” rows together. Consent, deletion and an honest text are needed now; an EU representative once the app is offered to people in the EU. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-27-gdpr/]

outside.title: If your team or company is outside the EU
items: Check whether the country has an EU adequacy decision. If it does (Switzerland, the UK, Japan and others), data flows as within the EU. If not, you need an Art. 46 tool, usually SCCs and a transfer impact assessment (TIA). [data https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/adequacy-decisions_en]

Contractor or your own product. A processor for an EU customer pays mainly for a DPA, SCCs and security. Your own product for people in the EU adds a representative under Art. 27 and the full controller set. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-3-gdpr/]
outside.countries: Specifics for each country, including transfers to a team there, are on the map.

representative.title: EU representative under Art. 27: what it is, when you need one, what it costs

what.title: What it is
items: A person or company in an EU country that an operator outside the EU appoints in writing as its contact for regulators and people (Art. 4(17), 27). The representative sits in a country where your users are (Art. 27(3)). [data https://gdpr-info.eu/art-27-gdpr/]

They receive requests and letters, show the records of processing (Art. 30) when a regulator asks, and pass everything on to you. Your obligations and liability for the data do not move to them (Art. 27(5)). [data https://gdpr-info.eu/art-27-gdpr/]

when.title: When you need one
items: If you have no establishment in the EU and GDPR applies to you through Art. 3(2): you offer services to people in the EU or monitor their behavior. [data https://gdpr-info.eu/art-3-gdpr/]

Not needed only if processing is at the same time occasional, excludes large-scale processing of special categories or criminal data, and is unlikely to create risk (Art. 27(2)). A service built on sensitive answers usually does not fit this exemption. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-27-gdpr/]

Swiss law requires a representative only from foreign operators (nFADP Art. 14), so a Swiss operator does not need one for users in Switzerland. [data https://prighter.com/resources/laws/swiss-fadp/fadp/articles/article-14]

cost.title: What it costs and what happens without one
items: Public prices as of November 2026: the cheapest €490–600 a year, mid-range €1,000–2,500, top tiers up to about €4,750. [data https://www.dpo-consulting.com/gdpr-representative-basic]
An acquaintance in the EU can also be your representative, but regulators’ letters and people’s claims will go to them. [inference https://gdpr-info.eu/art-27-gdpr/]

The first fine specifically for having no representative: €525,000, the Netherlands, 2021 (Locatefamily.com), plus €20,000 for every two weeks of delay, capped at €120,000. [data https://autoriteitpersoonsgegevens.nl/nl/nieuws/boete-van-525000-euro-voor-locatefamilycom]

risks.title: What a mistake leads to, besides a fine [data https://jonesday.com/en/insights/2023/05/cjeu-clarifies-the-right-to-compensation-for-gdpr-infringements-causing-nonmaterial-damage]

verdicts.title: Corrective order
verdicts.text: The regulator can ban processing, order data deleted, stop a transfer (Art. 58(2)).

verdicts.title: Claim by a person
verdicts.text: Compensation for non-material damage without a seriousness threshold; the damage must still be proven (C-300/21, 2023).

verdicts.title: Claim by a competitor
verdicts.text: EU countries may let competitors sue over GDPR breaches as unfair competition (C-21/23, 2024). Germany already does.

verdicts.title: Lost deals
verdicts.text: A corporate customer won’t sign without a DPA and answers on security. [inference https://curia.europa.eu/site/upload/docs/application/pdf/2024-10/cp240159en.pdf]

risks.sources: Jones Day on C-300/21, EU Court on C-21/23, BGH 2025

checks.title: How checks work
checks.lead: Nobody checks in advance. A regulator learns about you in one of three ways. [data https://rgpd.com/gdpr/chapter-8-remedies-liability-and-penalties/article-77-right-to-lodge-a-complaint-with-a-supervisory-authority]
inputs: A person’s complaintArt. 77, free, to the regulator where they live, work or where the breach happened. They don’t need to prove the breach first.
Your own breach noticeKnuddels reported a hack itself; the investigation found passwords stored in plain text.
The regulator’s own initiativeCoordinated EDPB actions; the 2026 topic is transparency and information.
checks.parallel: In parallel: a person can sue the company straight away (Art. 79, 82) without waiting for the regulator. If the regulator says nothing about a complaint for 3 months, you can sue the regulator itself (Art. 78). NGOs like noyb file complaints on people’s behalf (Art. 80).
checks.note: From 2 April 2027 cross-border cases get binding deadlines (Regulation 2025/2518).

cases.title: Modest fines [data https://www.enforcementtracker.com/ETid-1]
items: Austria, 2018. A betting shop filmed the pavement and car park and put up no CCTV sign.

Germany, 2018. The Knuddels chat stored passwords in plain text. According to the regulator, data of about 330,000 users was stolen; other sources give higher numbers. The amount was reduced for quick cooperation.
Germany, 2019, a private person. An email where all recipients saw each other’s addresses.
Private persons. At least 65 fines by October 2022, mostly for cameras at home and other people’s photos on social media.

who.title: Who gets fined and for what [inference https://cms.law/en/int/publication/GDPR-Enforcement-Tracker-Report/executive-summary]
who.small: Small businesses and private personsHundreds to tens of thousands of euros. Cameras, mailings without consent, a letter to the wrong recipient, no information for people, weak security exposed after a breach.
who.big: Big TechHundreds of millions of euros. Data transfers out of the EU, advertising without a legal basis, children’s data.

skills.title: Check your product against this page with a single sentence to your AI agent
skills.lead: Three open skills read your code, trace every personal-data flow down to the file and line, decide which laws apply and bring ready fixes. They send, delete and commit nothing without your “yes”.
skills.note: Works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot and Cursor. In Claude.ai, upload each folder from skills/ in the skills section of settings. MIT license.

chat.label: The AI agent’s answer with the skills
chat.question: Check journal-app for GDPR and nFADP, it’s already live.
answer: Possible incident. Journal entries and photos are open to outsiders. Close access first (fix #1), then check the logs.
Laws: nFADP and GDPR Art. 3(2)(a): sign-up offers Switzerland and Germany [code: signup/page.tsx:34] [inference].
findings: Blocker. Any signed-in user reads other people’s entries [code: init.sql:33]
Blocker. The photo bucket is public [code: storage.sql:2]
chat.caption: Based on a blind-test answer, shortened. The full report with tables and patches goes into a private document.
